title: Isomalt: What It Is, How Many Calories It Has, and How It Differs From Isomaltulose

seo.title: Isomalt: Calories and How It Differs From Isomaltulose
seo.meta_description: Isomalt is a sugar alcohol made from sucrose through isomaltulose and hydrogenation. FDA uses 2 calories per gram for labeling. It is less sweet than sugar, useful in hard candy, and only partly absorbed, so larger amounts can cause gas or diarrhea. It is not the same as isomaltulose.
seo.search_intent: Understand what isomalt is, how it is made, how many calories it provides, why confectioners use it, and how it differs from isomaltulose.

excerpt: Isomalt is a bulk sugar alcohol used mainly in hard candy, decorative sugar work, and sugar-free confectionery. It is manufactured from sucrose: sucrose is first converted to isomaltulose and then hydrogenated into a mixture of polyols. FDA uses 2 kcal/g for U.S. labeling. Unlike isomaltulose, isomalt is not fully digested and larger amounts can produce laxative gastrointestinal effects.
content_html:
Isomalt is a bulk sugar alcohol made from sucrose and used especially in sugar-free confectionery. It is less sweet than sugar, provides fewer calories, and is only partly absorbed.

Its name is easy to confuse with isomaltulose, but the two ingredients have different chemistry and digestive behavior.

How isomalt is made

The process begins with sucrose. An enzymatic step rearranges the glucose-fructose bond to form isomaltulose.

The isomaltulose is then hydrogenated, producing a mixture of two related disaccharide alcohols containing sorbitol- and mannitol-type structures.

The finished material is stable, relatively low in hygroscopicity, and crystallizes well for hard candy applications.

How many calories does isomalt provide?

FDA uses a specific factor of 2.0 calories per gram for isomalt on U.S. Nutrition Facts, about half the 4 calories per gram used for ordinary digestible carbohydrate.

The lower energy value reflects incomplete small-intestinal absorption.

Material reaching the colon can be fermented, producing some energy as short-chain fatty acids while also generating gas.

Why confectioners like isomalt

Isomalt provides bulk and structure while being less sweet than sucrose. It melts and hardens in a way that works well for transparent candy, lollipops, and decorative sugar pieces.

It also absorbs less moisture from the air than many conventional sugars, helping decorative pieces remain hard and less sticky.

Its lower cariogenic potential makes it useful in sugar-free confectionery as well.

Why can isomalt cause GI symptoms?

Incomplete absorption leaves part of the dose inside the intestinal lumen, where it holds water osmotically.

Colonic bacteria ferment some of the remaining polyol and generate gas. Large servings can therefore cause flatulence, rumbling, cramps, and diarrhea.

Confectionery trials show a dose-response relationship, with more symptoms at larger isomalt intakes than with sucrose in some consumers.

Isomalt is not isomaltulose

Isomaltulose is a digestible glucose-fructose disaccharide with an alpha-1,6 bond. It is hydrolyzed more slowly than sucrose but is ultimately absorbed almost completely.

Isomalt is the hydrogenated product derived from isomaltulose and belongs to the sugar-alcohol family. That is why it has fewer calories and more laxative potential.

The similar names describe related manufacturing chemistry, not interchangeable nutrition.

Blood glucose and dental effects

Because isomalt is incompletely absorbed, it produces a much smaller glucose response than sucrose.

Oral bacteria also do not ferment it as readily into enamel-demineralizing acids.

This can make it useful in sugar-free candy, but candy remains a discretionary food even when the carbohydrate source changes.

How much is tolerated?

There is no universal symptom threshold. Human studies indicate that single doses in the tens of grams can produce GI effects in some unadapted people.

Smaller servings, gradual exposure, and avoiding large combinations of multiple polyols generally improve tolerance.

The practical rule: isomalt is useful for sugar-free confectionery because it provides bulk with fewer calories, but incomplete absorption is also what limits comfortable serving size.

faq.question: How many calories does isomalt have?
faq.answer: FDA uses 2 calories per gram for U.S. labeling.

faq.question: Are isomalt and isomaltulose the same?
faq.answer: No. Isomalt is a partly absorbed sugar alcohol, while isomaltulose is a digestible glucose-fructose sugar.

faq.question: Can isomalt cause diarrhea?
faq.answer: Yes. Larger amounts can retain water in the intestine and ferment, producing gas and laxative effects.
